name: Hammer bonesmashing

card.summary: The claim that striking the face with a hammer or hard object will remodel facial bone into a sharper, more chiselled jaw and cheekbones.
card.note: Surgeons warn of fractures, nerve injury and lasting deformity; widely described as mostly a joke or online performance.

quick.overview:
Bonesmashing is a looksmaxxing concept in which a person hits their face with a hammer or other hard object, with the aim of a more chiselled jawline or cheekbones. Believers' reasoning draws on the idea that bone strengthens under stress and that injured bone heals back thicker.

In 2023 it spread as a TikTok and X trend, and coverage describes most of the content as satire or warnings. Doctors quoted in news and encyclopedic coverage say it does not improve appearance and can seriously injure.
quick.how: Because of the harm potential, no method is described here. Discussion online is mostly commentary, memes and warnings; Wikipedia calls it an inside joke that is rarely actually done. People who want a stronger-looking jaw are directed by clinicians to medically supervised options.
quick.risks: Doctors cite fractures, swelling, nerve damage, scarring, bite and tooth problems, facial misalignment and lasting deformity that can become more noticeable with age, and sometimes need emergency surgery. Surgeons say the idea that broken bones heal stronger misreads Wolff's law.

lead: Bonesmashing is a looksmaxxing practice, or claimed practice, of hitting the face against hard objects such as a hammer to produce a chiselled look. Wikipedia describes it as an inside joke that is rarely actually done [1].

The hashtag spread on TikTok and X in October 2023; a Futurism report said most posts were satire or warnings, with a small subset from looksmaxxing proponents, and that there was no evidence the practice was actually happening [2]. Know Your Meme, cited there, dates looksmaxxing forum culture to at least 2018 [2].

Believers' rationale is that bone responds to stress and heals thicker. Doctors say this partly misreads Wolff's law, which holds that bone adapts to load, and that the practice is unsafe [2]. A Brisbane plastic surgeon said it does not translate to improved appearance [3].

chain: Claimed bone remodelling as it heals
angle.text: Proponents claim trauma makes facial bone remodel into a sharper shape. Surgeons say it does not improve appearance and can cause lasting damage.

paras: Proponents say stress on bone leads it to rebuild denser and more defined, citing Wolff's law. Doctors quoted by Futurism say the notion that broken bones regrow stronger comes from a partial misreading of that law [2].

Futurism reported that the trend emerged in the weeks before 19 October 2023, that no originator was identified, and that most TikTok content under the hashtag was satire or warnings [2]. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article places it under hardmaxxing and calls it a rarely performed inside joke labelled misinformation by sources [4].

An emergency doctor, Josh Trebach, called it unsafe with no evidence it works [2]. Dr Diana Kennedy of Mater Private Hospital Brisbane warned of swelling, small fractures, worsening scars, nerve injury, emergency surgery, lasting deformity and bite problems [3]. Surgeons also cite misalignment, neurovascular injury and vision changes [4].
Coverage links the trend to appearance anxiety and to the broader looksmaxxing subculture; Futurism compared the dysmorphia to that in pro-anorexia communities [2].

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing forum culture dated to at least this year by Know Your Meme, per Futurism [2].
Bonesmashing spreads on TikTok and X [2].

lore.intro: Discussion is mostly in public media; Futurism and Wikipedia characterise much of it as satire and inside joking [1][2].

claims.claim: Hitting facial bone makes it grow back thicker and sharper.
claims.believers: Proponents invoke Wolff's law, that bone strengthens under stress [2].
claims.experts: Doctors say this misreads Wolff's law and that the practice risks fractures and deformity [2][3].
